tip: The accent on μού (moú) marks 'to me': μού σύστησε (moú sýstise) = he recommended to me. Unaccented μου (mu) is possessive: ο γιατρός μου (o yatrós mu) = my doctor.
Πήρα (píra) by itself means 'I phoned': πήρα τον μεσίτη (píra ton mesíti) = I called the agent. Greek drops the τηλέφωνο (tiléfono) – 'taking' someone is calling them.
Θέλει (théli) literally means 'it wants': θέλει δουλειά (théli douliá) = it wants work, i.e. it needs work. Greek things want repairs, painting, cleaning.
Στρώνω (stróno) means 'lay flat, smooth out', so έστρωσε (éstrose) = it smoothed into working order. Works for hinges, machines, even the weather.
Greek weather HAS its temperature: έχει σαράντα βαθμούς (éhi saránda vathmús) = 'it has forty degrees'. Degrees talk runs on έχει (éhi), not 'is'.
Δεν έκλεισα μάτι (den éklisa máti) is literally 'I didn't close an eye' – Greek counts a single eye where English counts a wink.
Μη βγαίνεις (mi vyénis) with the present stem = a standing rule: never go out in such heat. For just this once, Greek switches stems: μη βγεις (mi vyis).
Rain finds you in Greek: μας βρήκε η βροχή (mas vríke i vrohí) uses βρίσκω (vrísko = to find). Bad weather, news, and trouble all 'find' their victims.
Greek doubles a word for 'gradually': σιγά σιγά (siɣá siɣá) = little by little, from σιγά (siɣá = slowly). Same trick: λίγο λίγο (líɣo líɣo) = bit by bit.
Greek has no infinitive – where English says 'started to get cold', Greek conjugates both verbs: άρχισε να κρυώνει (árhise na krióni) = it started that-it-gets-cold.
Γιορτάζω (yiortázo) = I'm celebrating my name day – and that means open house. People drop by uninvited on name days; the invitation here is just a courtesy.
Της Παναγίας (tis Panayías), Aug 15, is the shared name day of every Μαρία (María) and Παναγιώτης (Panayótis) – one feast, thousands of celebrants.
Να (na) + verb turns a statement into a wish: να χαίρεσαι (na hérese) = may you enjoy. Greek blessings run on this pattern – να ζήσεις (na zísis) = may you live long.
The celebrant treats everyone: όποιος γιορτάζει (ópios yiortázi = whoever celebrates) φέρνει γλυκά (férni ɣliká = brings sweets) – the reverse of the English birthday norm.
Μεγάλη Παρασκευή (Meɣáli Paraskeví) is literally 'Great Friday' – a mourning day with the year's strictest fast, which is why κρέας (kréas = meat) is off the table.
Αληθώς Ανέστη (Alithós Anésti = truly He is risen) is the fixed reply to the Easter greeting Χριστός Ανέστη (Hristós Anésti) – a set call-and-response, not a free choice of words.
Μελομακάρονα (melomakárona, honey cookies) vs κουραμπιέδες (kurabiéðes, sugared almond ones) splits every Greek household at Christmas – picking a side is practically mandatory.
The -άκια (-ákia) ending shrinks things affectionately: φώτα (fóta = lights) → φωτάκια (fotákia) = little Christmas lights. Same move: σπίτι (spíti) → σπιτάκι (spitáki).
Ο Άι-Βασίλης (o Ai-Vasílis) is St. Basil, not St. Nicholas – his feast is Jan 1, so Greek gifts arrive την Πρωτοχρονιά (tin Protohroniá = on New Year's Day), not at Christmas.
Το πρώτο κομμάτι (to próto komáti = the first slice) of the New Year cake follows a fixed order: Christ first, then the house, then the absent, then everyone by age.
Εύχομαι (éfhome = I wish) sends wishes with a bare clitic: σου εύχομαι (su éfhome) = I wish you. No 'to' needed – the little σου (su) carries the whole 'to you'.
Απόκριες (Apókries = Carnival) grows an adjective with -ιάτικο: αποκριάτικο πάρτι (apokriátiko párti) = carnival party. Christmas things are χριστουγεννιάτικα (hristuɣeniátika).
Σαρακοστή (Sarakostí = Lent) is built on σαράντα (saránda = forty) – the name literally counts the 40 days that Καθαρά Δευτέρα (Kathará Ðeftéra = Clean Monday) opens.
The Lenten fast bans animals with blood, so θαλασσινά (thalasiná = seafood like shellfish) and ελιές (eliés = olives) pass while meat and dairy don't.
The ξανα- (ksana-) prefix means 'again': θα σε ξαναπάρω (tha se ksanapáro) = I'll call you again, i.e. call you back. It glues onto almost any verb – ξαναλέω (ksanaléo) = say again.
Κοντεύει να (kondévi na) is literally 'it nears to', from κοντά (kondá = near) – Greek's 'about to'. Κοντεύει να τελειώσει (kondévi na teliósi) = it's about to run out.
Άσε (áse), from αφήνω (afíno = to leave), builds 'let' commands with να (na): άσε το κινητό να φορτίσει (áse to kinitó na fortísi) = leave the phone to charge, i.e. let it charge.
Lights in Greek are lit, not switched: άναψε (ánapse) comes from ανάβω (anávo = light, ignite), the verb for a φακός (fakós = flashlight), lamps, and fires alike.
Ξέρω από (kséro apó) is literally 'I know FROM' – Greek's 'to be good with': δεν ξέρει από τεχνολογία (ðen kséri apó tehnoloɣía) = he's no good with technology.
'Everything that' is όλα όσα (óla ósa) – literally 'all as-many-as'. The English instinct όλα που (óla pu) sounds off: quantities take όσα (ósa), not που (pu).
Greek takes a photo OUT: βγάζεις μια φωτογραφία (vɣázis mia fotoɣrafía) uses βγάζω (vɣázo = take out, extract), not παίρνω (pérno = take).
After emotion verbs the 'that' is που (pu), not ότι (óti): χαίρομαι που σε βλέπω (hérome pu se vlépo) = I'm glad that I see you. Joy, sadness, and anger all take που.
Με στενοχώρησε (me stenohórise) = it upset me – the thing acts on you. The middle form στενοχωριέμαι (stenohoriéme) = I get upset – same verb, direction flipped.
Βαριέμαι (variéme = I'm bored) only exists in the passive-looking -μαι (-me) form. Greek feeling verbs often take this shape: κοιμάμαι (kimáme = I sleep), φοβάμαι (fováme = I fear).
Βαριέμαι (variéme) alone = I'm bored. Add να (na) + verb and it shifts: βαριέμαι να μαγειρεύω (variéme na maɣirévo) = I can't be bothered to cook. One verb, two meanings.
Φοβήθηκα (fovíthika) = I got scared, one specific fright – the one-time past of φοβάμαι (fováme = I'm afraid). Greek splits one-off events from ongoing states in the verb itself.
Ας (as) + verb = 'let's': ας μη μαλώνουμε (as mi malónume) = let's not fight. The μη(ν) (mi(n)) slots straight in for the negative – no extra 'do' or 'don't' machinery.
The liked thing is the subject, so plural things flip the verb: μου αρέσουν τα βίντεο (mu arésun ta vídeo) = the videos please me. One thing would take αρέσει (arési).
A να (na) clause counts as one single thing, so it is always αρέσει (arési), never αρέσουν (arésun): μας αρέσει να ταξιδεύουμε (mas arési na taksiðévume) = traveling pleases us.
When the liker is a noun, σε (se) marks them: άρεσε σε όλους (árese se ólus) = it pleased to everyone. The food is the subject – the people just receive the pleasing.
Μου αρέσει που γελάς (mu arési pu yelás) = I like that you laugh – που (pu) points at a real fact. Να (na) instead would mean liking the idea of laughing in general.
Λυπητερό (lipiteró) = sad, for things like a movie's τέλος (télos = ending). Sad people are λυπημένοι (lipiméni) – Greek splits what causes sadness from who feels it.
After από (apó) the pronoun goes to its object form: πιο ψηλός από εμένα (pio psilós apó eména) = taller than me. Εγώ (eɣó = I) never follows από – εμένα (eména) does.
Δικός (ðikós = own) agrees like an adjective: η δική μου (i ðikí mu) = mine, feminine to match η βαλίτσα (i valítsa = the suitcase). A masculine noun would make it ο δικός μου.
Καλύτερος (kalíteros) = better in one word – no πιο (pio) needed. Πιο καλύτερος doubles the comparison, like English 'more better'. Same with χειρότερος (hiróteros = worse).
